newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN SOCIALISTS VOW TO FORM NEW GOVERNMENT.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN SOCIALISTS VOW TO FORM NEW GOVERNMENT.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists look set to announce a new government on Monday despite 28 days of mass street demonstrations to demand immediate elections to resolve a political crisis and shore up a shattered economy.
The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) vowed to step up its protest campaign to force early elections if the Socialists did try to hang onto power by announcing a new cabinet.
UDF leader Ivan Kostov, addressing the daily opposition rally in Sofia, said on Sunday that the Socialists had "two choices, either to go in peace or to go in war, and we are prepared for both."

The Socialists, the ex-communists, made a last-ditch effort to woo President Petar Stoyanov and the UDF into talks on a crisis coalition to deal jointly with the collapsing economy, but Stoyanov and the UDF rebuffed them.

Socialist Party leader Georgi Parvanov said that, if the offer of coalition talks was turned down, the Socialists would name their cabinet on Monday and put it to parliament for a vote of confidence on Tuesday.
The constitution obliged Stoyanov to give the Socialists a mandate to form a government but the party has been divided over how to proceed in view of the mass demonstrations against its rule.

Students chanted anti-communist slogans outside party headquarters during a six-hour meeting of Socialist leaders on Sunday. They brandished effigies of Parvanov and Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the party's nominee for prime minister.
The UDF and student protesters who have staged strikes, rallies and blockades around the Balkan country for nearly a month vowed to step up their actions on Monday.
Bulgaria's government has been paralysed since December 21 when Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned in the face of widespread criticism.

As the economy disintegrated with an inflation rate jumping to 50 percent a month, urgent legislation, such as approving the 1997 budget or adopting measures to support the crumbling lev, has been left unattended.
The Socialists, elected to a four-year term in 1994, argue that a government must be appointed to deal with these matters first before holding elections later this year.
They have an absolute majority in parliament. Barring defections or a last-minute decision to give up the mandate, their cabinet should receive the required vote of confidence.
But if the Socialists do form a government, many people fear a repeat of the violence which broke out between police and protesters who besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10.

Protests by UDF supporters and workers are already dealing further blows to the economy. For five days, UDF supporters have cut road and rail links to Greece at Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia.
Dock workers at the Black Sea port of Varna called a strike starting from Monday and workers at Bourgas and other ports are expected to join it.

Miners and steelworkers have gone on strike and protesters have blocked main roads around the second city of Plovdiv. The distribution staff at the main Neftohim refinery is operating only a minimum service for schools, hospitals and police.
Student demonstrators blocked key road intersections in Sofia on Sunday, sitting down to play chess or cards. They wore badges saying: "The Game's Over."
